summary: Provides a framework for translating between IPv4 and IPv6, in the context of replacing NAT-PT (deprecated by RFC 4966) and letting both coexist during the move to IPv6. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A translator between two languages: devices that speak the new internet address language can talk to ones that speak the old one.

subtitle: How translators between IPv4 and IPv6 fit together, and which kind of translation suits which situation.

tldr.problem: Networks moving to IPv6 still need to talk to IPv4 systems, and NAT-PT, the earlier translation approach, was deprecated by RFC 4966 for its operational issues.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lays out eight translation scenarios and a framework of components: address translation, IP and ICMP translation, translation state, DNS64 and DNS46, and ALGs. It splits translators into stateless and stateful kinds and says which scenarios each can serve.
tldr.outcome: It points to companion documents for each component (RFC 6052, RFC 6145, RFC 6146, RFC 6147) and recommends translation as a temporary coexistence tool, not a permanent solution.

today: RFC 6144 is an Informational RFC published in April 2011, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the framework that the companion specifications RFC 6052, RFC 6145, RFC 6146 and RFC 6147 fill in.

sections.title: Why Translate Between IPv4 and IPv6
sections.content:
This note frames IPv4/IPv6 translation in the context of replacing NAT-PT (RFC 2766), which was deprecated by RFC 4966. The authors stress that the deprecation was not a claim that translation is bad; it was the way NAT-PT did it, and its use as a general-purpose solution, that was bad.

The IETF's preferred path, described in RFC 4213, is to deploy IPv6 alongside a stable IPv4 and switch IPv4 off when economics allow. Translation is for the cases where that is infeasible, for example when time or address supply runs short. The RFC contrasts it with tunneling, which lets users of the new protocol reach each other but does not let them communicate with old-protocol users without dual-stack hosts. It calls translation a medium-term coexistence strategy, not a long-term one.
sections.eli5: The best plan is for everybody to learn the new language. A translator is a temporary helper for when that cannot happen fast enough.

sections.title: Objectives and Key Terms
sections.content:
The RFC sorts applications into client/server applications, where clients start connections, and peer-to-peer applications, which both start and accept sessions. It wants clients to be able to open sessions to servers in either direction, ideally statelessly, and a stateful method is acceptable if complexity is minimized. It also aims to avoid, as much as possible, any software changes in hosts or applications.

The central distinction is state: dynamic information a translator keeps. A stateless translator derives what it needs from the packet and pre-configured information. A stateful translator creates or changes a data structure for each packet it handles. Two address types matter: IPv4-converted addresses represent IPv4 nodes inside an IPv6 network, and IPv4-translatable addresses are assigned to IPv6 nodes for stateless translation. Both rely on an explicit mapping to IPv4 addresses, using a prefix such as the Well-Known Prefix or a Network-Specific Prefix.
sections.eli5: A stateful translator keeps a notebook of who is talking to whom. A stateless one just follows a fixed rule on the label, so it needs no notebook.

sections.title: The Eight Scenarios
sections.content:
Translation cases are grouped by who is on each side: an IPv6 network to the IPv4 Internet, an IPv4 network to the IPv6 Internet, an IPv6 network to an IPv4 network, and the IPv6 Internet to the IPv4 Internet. Each splits by which side starts the communication, giving eight scenarios.

Scenario 1, an IPv6-only network reaching the IPv4 Internet, is the typical green-field case and can use stateless or stateful translation. Scenarios 2 and 4, starting from the IPv4 side, are described as hard cases; Scenario 4 is judged to occur only well past the early stage of the transition, so in-network translation is not considered viable there. Scenarios 7 and 8, between the two whole Internets, have no viable translation technique because of the difference in address space size.
sections.eli5: Who is calling whom, and from what kind of network, decides which kind of translator can help. Some of those situations are easy, some are hard, and a couple cannot be translated at all.

sections.title: Components of the Framework
sections.content:
The framework has five components. Address translation specifies how an IPv6 address maps to an IPv4 address algorithmically, as defined in RFC 6052. IP and ICMP translation converts packet headers, based on an update of the SIIT algorithm (RFC 2765), and is specified in RFC 6145. Translation state for stateful mode is covered by RFC 6146.

DNS64 turns an A record into a AAAA record, and DNS46 does the reverse; the preferred behavior is to translate only if no reachable record of the wanted type exists. See RFC 6147. Finally, some applications need an ALG; FTP is the example. A general rule is to run a server in each domain, or give one server an interface in each domain.
sections.eli5: A good translator needs several helpers: one to rewrite addresses, one to rewrite packet headers, one to remember conversations, one for the phone book (DNS), and special helpers for fussy programs.

sections.title: Stateless and Stateful Translation
sections.content:
In stateless translation, the translation information is carried in the address plus configuration in the translator. It permits sessions to start from either side, supports end-to-end address transparency, and scales better than stateful translation, but it constrains which IPv6 addresses can be assigned to nodes that use it. It can serve Scenarios 1, 2, 5 and 6.

In stateful translation, state is kept between IPv4 address and port pairs and IPv6 address and port pairs, so IPv6 systems can open sessions with IPv4 systems. Because of dynamic binding it generally supports only IPv6-initiated communication, and it does not give IPv6 nodes stable addresses for DNS. It can serve Scenarios 1, 3 and 5. Scenario 3 covers IPv4 servers, possibly on private RFC 1918 addresses, reached from the IPv6 Internet.

The RFC recommends using translation only temporarily for new parts of a network while IPv6 is brought up elsewhere, then turning off the unnecessary IPv4 service when economics warrant.
sections.eli5: The no-notebook translator works both ways but needs special addresses set aside. The notebook translator works with any address but mostly only for calls that start from the new-language side.

sections.title: Security and Open Problems
sections.content:
The framework defines no protocol of its own. Its Security Considerations section says that security issues are addressed in the individual translation documents, namely RFC 6052, RFC 6145, RFC 6146, RFC 6147 and the FTP64 draft.

The Unsolved Problems section is a single sentence: the framework does not cover all possible scenarios and may be extended in the future to address them.
sections.eli5: This note is a map, not a machine, so the safety details live in the documents for each piece. The map also admits it does not show every road.
